title: What Christian Nationalism Actually Is
subtitle: A definition built on the research, the lines that keep the word honest, and why the same idol waits on the other side of the aisle.

sections.title: The Word That Does Real Work
sections.body:
Christian nationalism became an insult before it became a definition, and that is a problem, because the thing it names is real and the slur it has turned into strikes people who do not deserve it. So begin with the careful version. The sociologists Andrew Whitehead and Samuel Perry, who have studied it more closely than almost anyone, define it as a cultural framework that fuses American civic life with a particular expression of Christianity, a belief that the nation is and ought to be Christian and that the government should act to keep it so. Philip Gorski and Perry sharpen the point. It is less a theology than a story about who the real Americans are and who gets to rule.

Notice what that definition does and does not say. It is not a description of Christian faith. It is a description of a political identity that borrows Christian symbols. A person can hold the entire Nicene Creed and reject Christian nationalism completely, and a person can wave every Christian symbol in the culture war while barely darkening a church door. The two are not the same axis. One is about what you believe concerning God. The other is about what you believe concerning the nation and the power to define it.

This distinction is the whole reason to write carefully instead of loudly. If Christian nationalism means nothing more than a Christian who votes, the word is a weapon against half the country and it should be retired. If it means something specific, a fusion of two loyalties into one, then the word matters, and the church of all places should want to know exactly where the line falls. Precision here is not pedantry. It is how you keep from slandering the faithful and excusing the idol in the same breath.

sections.title: The Spectrum, Not the Cartoon
sections.body:
The most useful thing the research did was refuse a yes-or-no answer. Working from the Baylor Religion Survey, Whitehead and Perry found that Americans do not split neatly into Christian nationalists and everyone else. They fall along a spectrum, and the two sociologists gave its four regions names. At one end are the Rejecters, who want a firm wall between faith and government and see the fusion as dangerous. Next are the Resisters, who lean that way but less absolutely. Then come the Accommodators, who lean toward blending faith and nation without going all the way. At the far end are the Ambassadors, who fully embrace the idea that America is a Christian nation and should be governed as one.

The spectrum matters because it kills the caricature. The Ambassador at the far end is a real position with real consequences, but most people who register some sympathy for Christian symbols in public life are Accommodators, not zealots plotting a theocracy. They are the grandmother who likes the manger on the courthouse lawn. Flatten that whole middle into the extreme and you have libeled tens of millions of people and learned nothing.

But the spectrum cuts the other way too, and honesty requires saying so. The far end is not a fantasy invented by nervous secularists. There is a genuine Ambassador position that does want political power to enforce a Christian social order, that does read pluralism as decline and difference as threat, and it has grown more articulate and more organized, not less. The data does two things at once. It shrinks the panic and it confirms the thing the panic was pointing at. A serious person has to hold both.

sections.title: What It Is Not
sections.body:
Before naming what Christian nationalism is, name three things it is not, because the word has been stretched to cover all of them and the stretch is dishonest.

It is not patriotism. Loving the country you were given, feeling gratitude for its genuine goods, grieving its failures as your own, wanting it to be just, none of that is idolatry. A man can love his mother without believing she is God, and he can love his country the same way. To brand ordinary patriotism as Christian nationalism is to leave a Christian no honorable way to love the place he lives.

It is not a Christian voting his conscience. When a believer carries convictions about human dignity or marriage or the poor into the voting booth, he is doing what every citizen does, reasoning from what he holds true to what he thinks the law should be. A secular activist does the identical thing from the other direction, and no one calls that a threat to democracy. Faith is not disqualified from public reasoning simply because it is faith.

And it is not the church seeking justice in public. When Christians fed the hungry, built the hospitals, marched against slavery and then against segregation, they were not smuggling in a theocracy. They were doing what the faith commands in the only world it has, the public one. A gospel with nothing to say about how we live together is not the gospel of the prophets or of Jesus.

Guard these three, or the word becomes useless, a club swung at any Christian who declines to keep his faith safely private. The line that matters is not between private faith and public faith. Every deep conviction goes public. The line falls somewhere else, and finding it is the only way to name the idol without slandering the worshipper.

sections.title: Why a Sincere Believer Is Drawn to It
sections.body:
Now the harder discipline. Before naming the idol, feel its pull, because a temptation you cannot feel is one you have not understood, and the people drawn to Christian nationalism are not monsters. They are, many of them, sincere believers watching something they love come apart.

Put yourself inside it. You raised your children in a moral world you believed was true and good, and that world is receding, mocked in the culture, contradicted in the school, absent from the screen. You remember when the country seemed to agree with you, or at least to make room for you, and now you feel like a stranger in the place your grandparents built. You are told your convictions are bigotry. You look at the vulnerable, the unborn, the addicted, the abandoned, and you believe the faith has answers the culture has thrown away. And you have a tool in your hand, the vote, the law, the state, and it seems not only permitted but responsible to use it to protect what is good and restrain what is evil.

That is not a stupid instinct. It is close to a Christian one. The desire that your nation honor God, that its laws bend toward the true, that your children inherit something better than confusion, is a distorted form of a right love. Augustine taught that evil is not a thing in itself but a good thing turned to the wrong end, a lower love that has climbed into the throne of a higher one. That is exactly what is happening here, and it is why the diagnosis has to be gentle. The problem is not that these people love too much. It is what the love gets attached to when fear gets hold of it.

sections.title: Where It Becomes Idolatry
sections.body:
Here is the line. Christian nationalism is not the love of country and it is not faith in public. It is the fusion of the two into a single loyalty, so that national identity and Christian identity become one thing, and the power of the state becomes the means by which the kingdom of God is supposed to arrive. That fusion is the idolatry, and it is idolatry precisely because it reverses the gospel it claims.

The kingdom Jesus preached does not come by seizing Rome. He said it to Pilate in the one sentence that should end the whole argument, that his kingdom was not of this world, for if it were, his servants would fight. It advances by the Spirit, by the cross, by witness and mercy and the slow patience of a mustard seed, not by capturing the machinery of the state and turning it against the neighbor. The moment the church decides the kingdom depends on who holds power, it has traded its actual weapon, the crucified God, for the very sword its Lord refused in the garden. Paul Miller, an evangelical who has argued this from inside the church, puts it plainly, that Christian nationalism takes a good thing, the ordering of public life, and makes it an ultimate thing, which is the classic anatomy of an idol.

There is a phrase for it I cannot improve on. The cross conscripted into a flag. Not politics. Idolatry. When the flag and the cross are sewn together, it is never the flag that ends up crucified. It is always the cross that ends up saluting. The nation does not get baptized. The faith gets nationalized, and a nationalized faith has always, in the end, blessed whatever the nation already wanted to do.

sections.title: The Mirror and the Plank
sections.body:
If this diagnosis only ever pointed right, it would be a partisan trick dressed as theology, so turn it on my own house. The fusion of faith and political power is not a sin of one wing. It is a human sin, and the left has its own liturgy for it. There the kingdom of God gets translated into a policy agenda, Jesus is recruited as the patron saint of a platform, and the church becomes a chaplaincy blessing whatever the movement had already decided. The symbols differ. The move is identical. A faith valued for its political usefulness, kept for the parts that vote correctly and quietly edited everywhere it offends the cause.

Kristin Kobes Du Mez traced how a particular white evangelical culture slowly fused its gospel with a vision of masculine, national strength until the two could not be pulled apart. The mechanism she describes is not unique to one side. Any tribe can do it. Any tribe can reach the point where it can no longer hear a word of Scripture its politics has not already approved, and that point, wherever it is reached, is the death of the prophetic and the birth of the idol.

I have stood in that place. I have preached the passage that flattered the room and left the one that would have cost me something on the study floor. I have wanted my side to win badly enough to let the wanting edit the text. The plank is in my eye before it is in anyone else's. That is why this cannot be a sermon aimed out the window at the other party. The seduction is the same on both altars, and the only church that can name it is one that has repented of it first. The flag is not the enemy. The idol is, and the idol will wear whatever colors the room is already cheering.
